Key supported: budgets-managing says 'alerted for both actual (after accruing) and forecasted (before accruing) spends' and that notifications can warn when you 'are forecasted to exceed' a cost or usage budget. Note that usage budgets also support forecasted notifications, but the wrong-option why correctly rests on the stem's monthly COST limit, so the option is still wrong.

Both keys are documented in one sentence of budgets-managing (notifications at 80 percent of the budgeted amount, plus an action that applies a custom IAM policy denying provisioning). Wrong options each fail one stated requirement and none can be defended as correct. Last wrong option (manual weekly check) is a strawman but acceptable.

Judged explicitly. The key (root user removes a bucket policy that denies all principals) is correct and documented. The first evidence quote ('Remove a misconfigured bucket policy that denies all principals from accessing an Amazon S3 bucket.') sits on id_root-user.html in the paragraph about privileged tasks performed on member accounts through centralized root access in AWS Organizations; the stem is a STANDALONE account, so the quote is on the wrong branch of the page. The same page's list of tasks that require root user credentials has the matching entry under Amazon Simple Storage Service Tasks: 'Edit or delete an Amazon S3 bucket policy that denies all principals.'

The wrong-option why 'An allow in an IAM policy does not override the bucket policy's deny for all principals' is supported by general policy evaluation logic (iam-eval-logic: 'An explicit deny in either of these policies overrides the allow'), not just for a deny on all principals; it is true but is not backed by any quote on this question, and the claim 'cannot remove it' for administrators is an inference from explicit-deny. The 'for all principals' wording is not a special rule; it is the explicit deny that wins. Supported if the explicit-deny quote is added.
No second defensible answer: a new IAM user or Identity Center admin is a principal covered by the deny.
suggestedFix: Replace evidence 1 with 'iam-root-user|Edit or delete an Amazon S3 bucket policy that denies all principals.' (keep 'Some tasks can only be performed when you sign in as the root user of an account.') and add 'iam-eval-logic|An explicit deny in either of these policies overrides the allow.' Reword the fourth wrong why to 'An explicit deny in a resource-based policy overrides any allow, so adding an allow does not remove the lock-out.'

Key and both quotes are verbatim on root-user-best-practices. The third wrong option (set a mail rule to forward to a colleague) is a weaker but legitimate near-miss: it still leaves the root email tied to the personal mailbox.

Both keys verbatim on root-user-best-practices. The 'store the password only in a tool inside the same account' why is supported by the same page ('Don't store the root user password with tools that depend on AWS services in an account that is accessed using that same password.').

Key is verbatim on iam-mfa ('MFA is enforced for all account types for their root user.' and 'including standalone accounts'). But the question is a meta documentation-recall item ('Which statement from the AWS documentation BEST describes the situation?'), not a scenario, and it turns on whether AWS has currently enforced root MFA, an enforcement/rollout status that can change and that the SAA exam does not test. Two of the wrong options ('only management accounts', 'only member accounts') are invented claims no one makes, so the item is near-trivial elimination.
A better formulation tests the durable principle (the root user of a standalone account should be protected with MFA) rather than the enforcement status.
suggestedFix: Rewrite as a scenario: 'A startup has created a standalone AWS account and wants to protect the root user. Which action meets this requirement?' correct: 'Register multi-factor authentication for the root user'; distractors: a longer password only, root access keys stored in a vault, sharing the password with the team. Keep the iam-mfa quotes ('You can enable MFA for the AWS account root user of all AWS accounts, including standalone accounts ...'). Or drop it, since 008 already tests root MFA.
